patient.chief_complaint: Progressive ascending quadriplegia with areflexia and bulbar weakness developing 20 hours after emergency PCI for acute MI, now requiring ICU transfer.
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Z. is a 73-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, prior ischemic stroke, and coronary artery disease who underwent emergency percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for an acute myocardial infarction 2 days ago. The MI was complicated by ST-elevation in the inferior, posterior, and right ventricular leads. Coronary angiography showed 90% stenosis of the proximal LAD, distal PL branch occlusion, and diffuse 85% stenosis of the mid RCA with thrombus autolysis. PCI was performed on the mid RCA. She was transferred to the cardiac ICU. Approximately 20 hours after the PCI, she was noticed to have bilateral upper limb weakness progressing from distal to proximal, with numbness. Over the following hours, weakness progressed to involve bilateral lower extremities and she became quadriplegic. She developed dysarthria and reduced pharyngeal reflexes bilaterally. Her SpO2 dropped to 93% and she required intubation. Cranial CT was performed and was unremarkable. The acute MI and PCI, with the stress of the procedure and the systemic inflammatory state, likely served as the triggering event for GBS. All standard viral serology (Mycoplasma, EBV, CMV, CMV antigenemia, HIV) was negative. Family initially refused LP due to the anticoagulation and clinical complexity, but LP was eventually performed and showed albumino-cytologic dissociation. Multiple ganglioside antibodies were identified: anti-GT1a, anti-GM1, and anti-GM2 IgG — this multi-antibody seropositivity strongly supports GBS in the absence of NCS and CSF confirmation.

quantitative_data.pattern: Severe AIDP with secondary axonal injury — low CMAP amplitudes indicate significant axonal degeneration

output.impression: Severe demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with secondary axonal injury. Markedly prolonged distal motor latencies, severely reduced conduction velocities, absent F-waves in all tested nerves, H-reflex absent. CMAP amplitudes markedly reduced in lower limb nerves indicating significant axonal degeneration. Absent sural sensory responses. Findings are consistent with severe acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with secondary axonal features. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, severe AIDP (post-MI/PCI trigger), multi-antibody seropositive (anti-GT1a, anti-GM1, anti-GM2), requiring mechanical ventilation

differential.key_features: CIP requires multi-organ failure and sepsis — not present at GBS onset; GBS preceded ICU admission; multi-antibody seropositivity specific to GBS
CIM requires prolonged high-dose NMJ blockers or steroids — not given; ascending weakness predated ICU
CT head normal; bilateral ascending pattern not stroke; areflexia not stroke; GBS antibodies strongly positive

optimal_actions.action: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days — initiated on clinical grounds (multi-antibody + CSF + clinical)
Labs including ganglioside antibody panel (GT1a, GM1, GM2)
Hold metoprolol if bradycardia — GBS autonomic dysfunction
ICU cardiac monitoring — post-MI + GBS = highest autonomic risk category

critical_actions: Hold metoprolol when bradycardia occurs — beta-blocker worsens GBS autonomic bradycardia; dual risk from GBS + post-MI autonomic instability
Multi-antibody seropositivity (GT1a + GM1 + GM2) allows clinical diagnosis of GBS without NCS when patient too unstable
Plasmapheresis is contraindicated — patient on triple antithrombotic therapy post-PCI; IVIG is the only feasible treatment
Atropine at bedside is mandatory — GBS bradycardia in post-MI context is particularly dangerous
Avoid QT-prolonging medications — QTc already 472 ms post-MI + GBS
contraindicated_actions: Succinylcholine for RSI — patient already intubated; if re-intubation needed use rocuronium
Plasmapheresis — contraindicated with triple antithrombotic therapy
key_reasoning_points: Acute MI and PCI are surgical/physiological stress triggers for GBS — the temporal relationship (GBS onset 20 hours post-PCI) is the key clinical clue
Multi-antibody seropositivity (GT1a + GM1 + GM2) allows Level 2 GBS diagnosis when NCS cannot be performed — ganglioside antibodies provide diagnostic certainty
Beta-blockers (metoprolol) must be held during GBS autonomic bradycardia — post-MI rate control with beta-blockers risks life-threatening bradycardia in GBS
Post-MI + GBS is the highest-risk autonomic scenario: two conditions each causing autonomic instability, combined with AF, triple antithrombotic therapy, and prolonged QTc
Critical illness polyneuropathy requires ICU multi-organ failure and sepsis — these were NOT present at GBS onset; GBS caused the ICU admission, not the other way around

red_herrings.data_point: Post-MI/PCI context with elevated procalcitonin 1.69 and BNP 526
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute neurological deterioration to sepsis, critical illness polyneuropathy, or embolic stroke from MI rather than GBS
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Procalcitonin elevation is post-procedure inflammatory response (blood cultures negative); CIP requires multi-organ failure; multi-antibody seropositivity and ascending neurological decline preceding ICU admission confirms GBS as primary diagnosis
